subject: geography
title: KS3 Geography - Glaciation Reading
description: Reading passages on glacier formation, glacial erosion, depositional landforms and the management of tourist pressure in glacial landscapes.

data.sourcePassage: A glacier is a large moving body of ice that flows slowly because of gravity. Glaciers form in places where more snow falls than melts. This build-up of snow is called accumulation. As layer after layer of snow piles up, the lower snow is compressed by the weight above it and becomes dense firn. Over hundreds of years, firn turns into glacier ice. The heavy ice then starts to move downhill. In warmer periods, melting called ablation may happen at the snout. If melting is faster than forward movement, the glacier retreats.

questions.question: What is the term for the build-up of snow where more falls than melts?
How does snow change into firn?
questions.modelAnswer: It is compressed by the weight of layers of snow above it until it becomes dense and compacted.

questions.question: Why does the glacier begin to move downhill?
questions.modelAnswer: The ice mass becomes very heavy, so gravity pulls it downhill.

questions.question: What does glacier retreat suggest about melting compared with forward movement?
questions.modelAnswer: It suggests that melting is happening faster than the glacier is moving forward.

data.sourcePassage: Glaciers shape the land by weathering and erosion. Freeze-thaw weathering happens when water gets into cracks in rock, freezes, expands and breaks the rock apart. Two important erosional processes are plucking and abrasion. In plucking, meltwater freezes around rocks at the base or sides of the glacier, and the moving ice pulls them away. In abrasion, rock fragments carried by the glacier scrape and polish the rock beneath. These processes help create corries, steep back walls and wider, deeper valleys. Over time, a river valley can be widened and straightened into a U-shaped valley.

questions.question: Which two processes are named as the main types of glacial erosion?
How is freeze-thaw different from plucking?
questions.modelAnswer: Freeze-thaw breaks rock apart in place, while plucking removes rock as glacier ice freezes around it and pulls it away.

questions.question: Why does abrasion help make valleys wider and deeper?
questions.modelAnswer: Because rocks carried by the glacier grind against the valley floor and sides, scraping away material.

questions.question: What evidence in a landscape might suggest past glaciation?
questions.modelAnswer: Features such as corries, steep back walls and U-shaped valleys suggest the landscape was shaped by glaciers in the past.

data.sourcePassage: When glacier ice melts, it drops the material it has been carrying. This deposited material is called moraine. Terminal moraine marks the furthest advance of the glacier, while lateral moraine is left along the sides. Medial moraine forms when two glaciers join and their side moraines combine. Drumlins are smooth hills shaped like half-buried eggs or teardrops. They point in the direction the glacier moved and often appear in groups called a drumlin field. Erratics are large rocks carried by the glacier and dropped far from their original source, sometimes on very different rock types.

questions.question: What is the name for material deposited by a glacier after melting?
How can terminal moraine help geographers understand the past glacier?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows the furthest point that the glacier reached before it retreated.

questions.question: Why do drumlins point in the direction of glacier movement?
questions.modelAnswer: Because the moving glacier streamlines the deposited material, tapering it in the direction of flow.

questions.question: Why might an erratic be a different rock type from the local area?
questions.modelAnswer: Because the glacier transported it from somewhere else and then dropped it after melting.

data.sourcePassage: Glacial landscapes attract many tourists because of their dramatic scenery and distinctive landforms, but they are also fragile environments. Places that attract large numbers of visitors are called honeypot sites. Tourism can create jobs and income, yet it can also damage vegetation, increase erosion on footpaths, disturb farm animals, and cause traffic congestion, noise and pollution. Overcrowding may also affect local people. Sustainable tourism means managing these competing pressures so the landscape can still be enjoyed in the future. Common responses include diverting walking routes, promoting public transport and cycling, keeping dogs on leads around farms, and using visitor centres to educate tourists.

questions.question: What is a honeypot site?
options: A place that attracts many tourists
A valley filled with glacier ice
A farm beside a mountain lake
questions.modelAnswer: A place that attracts many tourists

questions.question: Give one environmental problem caused by tourism in glacial landscapes.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples include vegetation being destroyed, footpath erosion, water pollution, air pollution or noise pollution.

questions.question: Why is sustainable tourism important in glacial landscapes?
questions.modelAnswer: Because these landscapes are fragile, so tourism must be managed carefully if future generations are to keep enjoying them.

questions.question: How do visitor centres and transport schemes help reduce conflict?
questions.modelAnswer: They educate visitors about responsible behaviour and reduce congestion by encouraging more sustainable travel choices.
